details: Tornadoes, Thunderstorm Winds, Hail, Storm Surge, Flooding, Beach Erosion, SnowThe "Storm Of The Century" roared across Florida producing a variety of severe and unusual weather conditions for a period of about 18 hours from late Friday the 12th through late afternoon Saturday the 13th.  A severe squall line raced eastward at 50 mph ahead of an intense low producing several tornadoes and strong downbursts as it moved through the state and directly caused seven fatalities.  This was followed by a hitherto unknown  (for the Gulf Coast) winter storm surge of 9 to 12 feet onto the gulf coast in Taylor County, with storm surges and/or tidal and wind driven flooding of 5 to 9 feet elsewhere along the gulf coast of the state and into the lower Keys.  This was followed by a period of 8 to 12 hours of high sustained winds of up to 50 mph with gusts to 70 mph, keeping tides much above normal along the west coast and causing severe beach erosion in many areas.  Total number of fatalities from the storm was 47, including 14 from storm surge and flooding, seven from tornadoes and/or strong downbursts, and four from high winds in the aftermath of the squall line.  Eleven people drowned offshore in the Gulf of Mexico after strong winds swamped or capsized ships  (including seven crewmen from a 200-foot Honduran freighter).  Eleven others died during rescue operations and cleanup activities.  Meanwhile, colder air poured in behind the intense low with up to four inches of snow falling in the panhandle from north of Pensacola to Crestview, and a trace to 3 inches elsewhere across north Florida.  Record or near record low temperatures occurred over much of the state the following two nights.  Total property damage was estimated at $1.6 billion.

A large tornado and its attendant vortices left a swath of destruction from northwest Minnehaha County through western Moody County into eastern Brookings County. Numerous farms and residences were destroyed or damaged and trees snapped off or uprooted. Around 1630 CDT multiple vortices formed into the tornado two miles west of Lyons destroying barns and silos and killing animals on several farms. Shortly after, the tornado leveled two houses, seriously injuring four people as they were buried in the rubble. It then caused destruction on at least 10 more farms before entering the northwest side of Colman at 1700 CDT. At least 15 homes in Colman had an estimated total of $250,000 in damage mainly due to the roofs either being blown off or trees falling on them. At 1710 CDT the tornado damaged houses and trees three miles north/northeast of Colman. Around 1715 CDT, 10 miles northwest of Flandreau, the tornado leveled a farm, except for the silo, and injured a man who received multiple pelvis fractures. On two farms, one 2 miles southwest of Aurora and the other 1 mile west of Aurora, buildings and grain bins were destroyed around 1735 CDT. The tornado then continued north/northeast, wrecking irrigation systems and uprooting and snapping off hundreds of trees, before causing destruction on another farm about 6 miles northeast of Brookings around 1745 CDT. Northeast of White, three farms sustained major damage to buildings and trees. Cows were also killed and power lines downed.

A large tornado tore a north/northeast path of destruction through at least 10 farms. On one farm southeast of Junius all that remained was the foundation and steps of the house and the bumper and engine of a pickup truck. On other farms livestock were crippled and a horse was impaled by a piece of wood. At least four people were injured as several vehicles were flipped by the tornado. A woman was driving on a highway west of Madison when the wind started spinning her car around and the windows shattered. About 200 power poles were downed leaving 2800 customers without electricity.

overview: As the low mentioned above continued to move northeast, the warm front pressed into Iowa and a dry line moved across the plains. Thunderstorms fired ahead of the dry line in northwest Iowa. The storms fired from a combination of the dry line and synoptic forcing. The first storms produced a 65 mph wind gust near Arnolds Park. The winds lifted boats from their moorings and overturned a couple of them. Several tornadoes were spawned by the storms. The strongest was in Lyon and Osceola Counties. The tornado was on the ground for about 10 miles. Though much of its path was over open country, the tornado did cause significant damage in Sibley. On its path, the tornado destroyed a cattle shed, blew out windows, and downed several trees. In Sibley, one roof was taken off of a house and a high school bus barn was taken down. Damage to the bus barn was around $150,000. There were several injuries in Sibley caused by flying glass and debris. Two other were injured as the collided while driving their cars in an attempt to outrun the tornado. Ironically, the call to action statement in the tornado warning for the area specifically advised NOT to try to outrun the tornado in your car. A second tornado was on the ground for about 7.5 miles. This tornado was not as strong, but did cause damage in Sioux County between Hospers and Sheldon. Several barns were taken down, along with a few silos. The tornado moved into the campus of the Northwest Iowa Community College, causing quite a bit of damage to the buildings. Other tornadoes touched down in the area in what turned out to be a small family of tornadoes. Damage was minor as the other tornadoes swept across open countryside. Lightning struck a house in Milford, starting a small fire.

A 28-mile long tornado wound its way across Marquette, Green Lake and Fond du Lac counties. The tornado set down 7 miles east southeast of Endeavor and moved northeast. It entered Green Lake County 5.5 miles southwest of Marquette and continued northeast through Marquette and along the southern shore of Green Lake. It entered Fond du Lac county 2 miles west of Ripon and crossed the north portions of the town before lifting. This tornado damaged 228 structures in Green Lake County and 30 more in Ripon, as well as knocking down numerous trees and power lines.

A strong tornado developed 3 miles south-southwest of Newkirk at 1635 CST and moved east-northeast 11.5 miles before dissipating at 1702 CST 10 miles east of Newkirk. This F3 tornado destroyed a two-story, five-bedroom brick house, a mobile home, three barns, a television tower, two out buildings, a motor home, a pop-up camper, a pole barn and a pole shed. The tornado downed trees and power lines and was between 100 and 250 yards wide.

A tornado destroyed an empty mobile home and laundrymat. Numerous windows were broken in homes and many trees were blown down. There was minor damage to some roofs and a shed was destroyed. Damage was estimated around $250,000.

From Everson to Wooddale, a tornado destroyed 3 mobile homes and two barns. One of the mobile homes overturned and injured a 45-year-old women. The second mobile home the roof tore off, which landed into a nearby fire station causing $20,000 in damage to the Bullskin Township fire station. A firemen at the station was injured by flying debris. Siding was torn from several other homes, and a porch roof was ripped from a house. A total of 23 homes, 9 mobile homes, 3 barns, a private school, and 1 business received minor damage. Along Route 1047, east of Scottdale, a 1,000 pound horse was seen flying through the air before landing in a nearby creek. The horse underwent surgery for an 8-inch gash to the chest. Five other horses were also fifted off the ground, and carried several hundred yards.

There was extensive damage at the Shady Lane Campground and Mobile Home Park southwest of Plymouth. A small tornado that touched down briefly in Sterling, Illinois. A car full of people sighted the tornado on Illinois State Route 2 and the corner of Woodlawn Road. Damage consisted of twisted trees, light poles, and a large swing set destroyed.
A tornado was spotted over the Ohio River. It lifted before reaching land.

The path began near route 60 and crossed Interstate 64 near exit 20. Minor damage occurred several roofs on buildings located around the Barboursville Mall. Signs were knocked down. Trees on the southwest and northeast side of White Chapel Cemetery were pulled from the ground and snapped off at the top. Damage along the narrow path was not complete, but indicated skipping.
In Piscataway a tornado touched down briefly, but no injuries were reported.

This small and short-lived tornado was first spotted near North Brandywine JHS and travelled southeast crossing route 30. The tornado veered southwest after crossing route 340 and dissipated in an area east of the Veterans Administration Medical Center. A funnel cloud was spotted aloft during a large portion of the route. The hardest hit area was apparently near Caln. Crews worked through the night to clear dozens of trees and branches, tangled wires, replace fallen utility poles and repair damaged transformers. The hospital was forced to us emergency generator power. Just down the road from the hospital, a barn built in 1812 was turned to rubble. The tornado pushed the silo about 6 inches off its base and collapsed the roof, crushing farm equipment inside. Newly planted crops were blown in all directions and there were 7,000 power outages throughout the county. An AT&T employee was killed when a falling tree struck his vehicle as he was driving north on North Caln Road about 1530 EST. The tree also snapped two electric wires on the way down, preventing rescue workers from getting to the man. (M45V)

The first tornado briefly touched down at 1558 CST near the intersection of U.S. Highway 75 and 141st Street South in Glenpool. The tornado damaged a lumber yard and 2 or 3 mobile homes in this area before lifting. Damage to the lumber yard was estimated at $150,000. The manager of the lumber yard sustained a broken hand. This tornado was rated F0 in intensity.

The second tornado touched down at 1600 CST 4 miles north northeast of Sapulpa. The tornado damaged a house, garage and trees on the north side of Interstate 44 before crossing the interstate and damaging a truck driving school. The tornado moved east into Tulsa County at 1605 CST and damaged several homes and one apartment near 61st Street South and 33rd West Avenue. Several vehicles were also damaged in this area. The tornado lifted at 1606 CST near the intersection of U.S. Highway 75 and 61st Street South. The 3-mile-long and 50-yard-wide damage path was not continuous, and the tornado produced F0 to occasional F1 damage.

The third tornado touched down at 1615 CST near the intersection of Kent and Lyons Streets in Broken Arrow. The tornado caused considerable damage to several homes in this area. This 50-yard-wide tornado was on the ground for less than 1/8 mile and produced F0 to F1 damage.
The fourth tornado touched down very briefly near Oneta at 1619 CST. This F0 tornado uprooted trees.

An F1 tornado touched down in the southeast part of Van Buren and traveled approximately 0.3 of a mile. Most of the damage consisted of one side and the roof of a storage warehouse being torn off. A trailer was overturned and several trees and power lines were also knocked down.
A small tornado was reported in Rockport. Several trees were uprooted and a mobile home was heavily damaged and a building lost part of it's roof.
A short lived tornado touched down and destroyed a mobile home, several garages, a few barns and downed several trees along its path.

A tornado, which formed at a location 14 miles south of Pocatello, skipped along a 10-mile-long path to the northeast, ending in Inkom, 13 miles southeast of Pocatello. The tornado did significant damage. Dozens of trees were uprooted and twisted. The tornado knocked over a grain elevator and overturned a semi truck. Several outbuildings were destroyed and numerous windows were broken out of buildings. Two minor injuries were reported, both attributed to falling limbs. An inspection of the storm site was completed by National Weather Service Personnel. This inspection revealed this tornado to be an F1 scale tornado based on the damage sustained. A small tornado moved through the community knocking down tree limbs and a few trees. Some damage was also reported to games and rides of a carnival which were set up on city street for a local celebration.

Two tornadoes, 50 miles northwest of Idaho Falls, were spotted by a U.S. Forest Service employee. Some damage was done to the metal roof of a trailer house. Another tornado, 35 miles northwest of Idaho Falls also caused minor damage to trees. Four funnel clouds accompanied the latter tornado.

details: A severe weather spotter reported a tornado 55 miles northwest of Idaho Falls. The tornado was on the ground for two minutes, then ascended and was visible as a funnel for another 30 minutes. No damage was reported.

Trees were uprooted, broken and twisted off in all directions. The damage was on top of a hill. An eye witness saw the tornado tear up the trees after heavy rain and half dollar-size hail had moved through the area.
A waterspout was observed 5 miles north of the Marathon airport.
A tornado touched down in a residential area near downtown where it tore off some house shingles. It moved to Tampa Bay before dissipating.
A tornado touched down in Bradenton blowing down a fence and downing a tree.
A spotter reported a small tornado southwest of Holyoke. The tornado touched down in an open field, and was on the ground for a short time. No damage or injuries was reported.
A likely tornado tossed two construction trailers and two trucks, and damaged two small buildings. Two men escaped with minor injuries.
A tornado touched down briefly in Wright County south of the Clarion Airport. Witnesses reported seeing the tornado pick up dirt as it touched down in an open field.
A waterspout was observed 5 miles south of Key West.
A brief tornado touchdown destroyed one outbuilding and overturned a grain silo.
This tornado touched down over open country and remained over open country until it dissipated.
This tornado touched down over open country, blew the siding off of a steel shed at one farmstead, and dissipated shortly thereafter.
This tornado touched down over open country, then destroyed the roof of a barn before dissipating.

The tornado set down north of Markesan on the south shore of Little Green Lake in Green Lake county. It caused $100,000 in damage to 26 buildings as well as knocking down numerous trees and power lines.
Baca County Sheriff reported a brief tornado touch-down in an open field southwest of Springfield. No damage or injuries was reported.
A tornado touched down briefly in rural Worth damaging several shed roofs and demolishing a barn. Time estimated from local newspaper reports.
The public reported a small tornado south of Lamar. The tornado touched down in an open field and was on the ground for about 10 minutes before dissipating. No injuries or damages were reported.
State patrol reported a brief tornado touchdown south of Eads. No injuries or damage was reported.

A lone thunderstorm developed in front of a line of thunderstorms. A tornado was reported by the public in open farmland. This tornado touched down briefly. The thunderstorm that produced this tornado continued to move to the east.

One barn was destroyed, however the hogs in the barn were able to escape. The tornado toppled over head stones in a cemetery southwest of Sigourney. The tornado briefly lifted as it crossed highway 149, then touched down and destroyed two out buildings and tore the side off an airplane hanger at the Sigourney Airport. Extensive damage was reported at the airport.

A tornado made a brief touchdown... damaging an industrial building. The front wall of the building was destroyed and a huge exhaust fan vent was torn from the roof... damage at the industrial site was estimated at $75,000.

A strong tornado touched down in Delaware County. The storm was tracked by weather radar as a mesocyclone. It touched down south and west of Manchester, causing major structural damage to a farm house. Later it picked up a car, spun it around, and turned it upside down north of Manchester. It moved into a forested area and finally lifted.

The third tornado was also quite strong. It touched down south of the Dubuque Airport. Tree branches fell out of the sky onto the runway at the Dubuque Airport. A large piece of sheet metal fell on top of the terminal building. A Northwest Airlink flight landed at the airport with tree branches attached to the aircraft. At least one farmstead was hit with a glancing blow. About $15,000 damage was reported with several propane tanks leaking following the damage caused by the tornado. The tornado tracked north-northeast across the extreme northwest tip of Illinois and into southwest Wisconsin where it finally dissipated.

An F3 tornado touched down in Iowa. It crossed the Mississippi River into Illinois at 1602 CST and crossed into Wisconsin at 1612 CST. It weakened to F1 intensity and had a skipping path over northwest Jo Daviess County. Minor damage to trees and outbuildings occurred at a farm near Menominee.

A cluster of severe thunderstorms deposited hail up to golfball size, and spun very weak tornados across southern Wisconsin. Three tornadoes were sighted in Grant County near Sinsinawa, Platteville and Georgetown... The storms caused minor tree and power line damage.
Three tornadoes were sighted in Grant County near Sinsinawa, Platteville and Georgetown... The storms caused minor tree and power line damage.

Another tornado was spotted 5 miles southwest of Belmont in Lafayette County. The storms caused minor tree and power line damage.
A small, brief tornado destroyed a 600 pound kennel fence about 0.25 miles southeast of the Lake Charles National Weather Service Office.

A F0 tornado moved through the Sterling Heights area... Pieces of steel plating from Bond robotics were moved from their original location... Scaffolding fell and was twisted. A 3-inch-diameter limb was driven into the ground.
A small tornado touched down in Potsdam uprooting trees, destroying a satellite dish and a large wooden jungle gym.
At Califon, in Hunterdon County, a tornado touched down briefly but no injuries were reported.
A spotter on Hauser Lake saw a waterspout come ashore and overturned some picnic tables.
A tornado touched down on the Meadowlark Golf Course and destroyed a tree and damaged the club house. A car dealership on the east end of Great Falls received damage.
A tornado touched down briefly and dissipated near the town of Bagely.

overview: Three or four funnel clouds were reported and two tornados touched down south and southeast of Bridgeport. One tornado tore out 100 yards of fence and upset an irrigation system. Another tornado uprooted more than 100 pine trees.

details: A tornado touched down in an open field with no damage.

overview: At least two small torndoes and a funnel cloud were noted in northeast Wyoming. No injuries or damage from either tornado with both in open fields.

details: A small tornado damaged a house roof in Jacksonville.

details: A weather spotter reported a brief tornado touch down southeast of Akron. He described it as a ground-based swirl of dust with no apparent connection to the base of the storm. No injuries or damage was reported.
A small tornado scattered backyard furniture in LaBelle.
A tornado damaged tree limbs before dissipating.
A tornado briefly touched down in open country. Spotters reported no damage.
A tornado touched down briefly at Chappell. Golfball-size hail was also reported.
A brief tornado touchdown 4 miles west of Wing destroyed sections of fence.
A NWS employee spotted a tornado near Chappell. The tornado was short lived and caused no apparent damage.

overview: Spotters reported a brief tornado west of Big Springs. Another tornado touched down briefly north of Big Springs from the same thunderstorm.
Spotters reported a brief tornado west of Big Springs. Another tornado touched down briefly north of Big Springs from the same thunderstorm.

details: A waterspout was observed 4 miles north of Key West.
Tornado moved 10 mph east-southeast over open country.
A brief tornado touchdown blew out windows and tipped a wagon.

Tornados and high winds crossed Edmunds County between 2100 CDT and 2200 CDT. At 2100 CDT, the tornado destroyed a building west of Bowdle. The tornado lifted before moving over Bowdle but high winds still toppled trees, one of which crushed a car.
Similar damage occurred in the Roscoe area. West of Roscoe a grain bin was destroyed and a farm building damaged by tornadic winds.
A tornado and high winds damaged buildings on several farms in the Redfield, Athol, and Ashton areas.
Tornado of waterspout origin came from inlet side and tore off or damaged roofs of four homes. Furnishings were smashed against walls and furniture was strewn about by the winds.
A tornado touched down briefly near Nielsville.

overview: At least four waterspouts were observed over Tampa Bay between St. Petersburg Beach and Longboat Key.

details: A tornado was spotted north of Alliance. The tornado destroyed a pump house.
A waterspout was observed 6 miles west of the Key West airport.

A tornado and winds reported at 95 mph destroyed or damaged buildings on at least six farms and downed power lines in the Dixon area. Hail also stripped crops and made the ground white in some locations. Up to 4.00 inches of precipitation was reported, which flooded small streams and stock dams.
A tornado was spotted by a sheriff's deputy northwest of Anton. The short-lived tornado touched down in an open field, with no damage or injuries reported.
A waterspout was observed just off the Lake Worth Inlet.
Weak tornadoes formed just north of Lovell at 1625 CST. This F0 tornado developed over open fields and no damage was reported.
Weak tornadoes formed... 3 miles north-northwest of Crescent at 1650 CST [sic: table says 1647-. This F0 tornado developed over open fields and no damage was reported.
A waterspout was observed 2 miles north of the Key West airport.

A waterspout formed over Newfound Harbor and moved northwest onshore at Merritt Island airport. It overturned three single engine aircraft and destroyed eight ultralights. It then moved into an industrial area where it blew over a few trees and destroyed a warehouse roof before disappearing in the Indian River.
State Police reported a tornado on the ground in a rural area near town.
State Police reported a brief touchdown.
A small tornado was witnessed touching down briefly in Pittsfield. It knocked down one tree and damaged a few others at the courthouse. Windows were blown in at a store in town.
A small tornado moved across Siesta Key ripping sheet metal roofing from a building. A car window was knocked out by flying debris.
A tornado touched down briefly just north of Clovis at 1515 MST. It destroyed a small shed constructed of wood and tin.
A waterspout-tornado on an intermittent path made landfall in Metairie where it damaged trees and the roofs of about 13 homes.
A brief tornado was reported over open country.
A tornado briefly touched down near Arcadia.
A tornado moved south at 40 mph.
The Texas Department of Safety reported a brief tornado seen by 12 citizens near the intersection of Highway 35 and Farm-to-Market Road 128 near Pearland.
A tornado was spotted just south of Cushing moving northeast. Heavy crop damage was noted just east of Cushing.
A tornado moving south left an intermittent path in open country. Power lines were knocked down 8 miles south of Broken Bow.
A brief tornado was reported over open country.
A tornado briefly touched down just west of Rockville.
A small tornado touched down briefly at the Illinois-Wisconsin state line at Route 14. An office trailer was damaged.
A 5-mile long tornado track caused little damage as it skipped from near Sharon to Walworth in Walworth county.
A small tornado briefly touched down just south of Argyle in Lafayette County.
A third tornado wrecked some trees and power lines near Twin Lakes in Kenosha County.

Many roofs to homes and mobile homes were damaged or destroyed on the east side of Garden City. Two mobile homes were knocked off their foundations. A semi trailer truck was knocked over. Six hanger doors at the Garden City Airport were blown off. One hangar door was blown into a Aerostar airplane parked inside the hangar. A modular classroom at Victor Ornlelas Elementary School was knocked off its foundation.
A small tornado struck Crescent Beach uprooting trees and peeling roofing off a storage shed and two houses. Golf carts being kept in the storage shed were also damaged.

A short lived tornado touched near the intersection of U.S. Highway 17 and Georgia Highway 303. The tornado twisted off the tops of several large pine trees and removed a roof from a small building along its path.
High winds near a tornado snapped off large trees, tipped over propane tanks, and tore a roof off a trailer.

A small tornado touched down near Lees Creek and moved southeast into Highland County at about 1356 EST. The tornado, which was witnessed and filmed by a citizen, was not on the ground the entire pathlength, and moved through a rural area. Trees were downed and minor damage occurred to a home and several outbuildings.

A tornado touched down in Pulteney in Steuben County around 1900 EDT. The tornado first touched down and damaged a garage, trailer and porch and moved a grill and picnic table about 100 feet... The tornado lifted off the ground and touched down again in a wooded area. There was considerable tree damage in this area with most of the trees broken about a third of the way up. The tornado lifted again and on its final touchdown appeared to do the most damage. The siding and gutters were torn off a house and a motor boat was picked off its trailer and moved about 20 feet. A trailer also suffered substantial damage and a large wooden shed was badly damaged. A large tractor inside the shed was moved about 10 feet. A husband and wife were injured by flying debris as they unsuccessfully attempted to reach a storm cellar under the barn.

The county EOC reported a tornado touchdown along Highway CC between Racine and Highway 60. A large oak tree fell damaging two cars and a house along Highway CC. One person received minor cuts from flying glass when the storm broke windows out. A nearby mobile home was also damaged while numerous trees were knocked down along the path.

A tornado was observed by persons in Cement Ridge Lookout 1 mile inside the Wyoming/South Dakota border. The tornado moved east into South Dakota with little or no damage in Wyoming. See Storm Report for South Dakota.

A strong tornado crossed the Wyoming/South Dakota border near Cement Ridge and Tinton, South Dakota. Winds of 112 mph were recorded at a nearby lookout tower. The tornado took out a wide swath of large pine trees in the forest on a hillside. Afterwards the U.S. Forest Service had to clear the roads that were full of fallen trees.
A waterspout was observed 2 miles east of Melbourne.
A short lived and weak tornado touched down near the eastern banks of the Chattahoochee River and skipped east with little damage. A few trees were twisted off at the crowns.

overview: Several tornadoes were spawned during the evening. Most of them were brief touch downs and caused little damage. Such was the case in Greene County, where two brief touch downs occurred in open countryside. An earlier touch down north of Sibley, in Ocseola County, did little more than cause tree damage. Two tornadoes touched down in Pocahontas County. The first was a brief touch down. The second was on the ground between Havelock and Gilmore City. Much of the area it traversed was open country. A few farmsteads were affected with most damage to out buildings. One farmstead received significant damage northwest of Gilmore City just before the tornado lifted. The storm was still strong as it moved across the city. Damage was substantial at a lumber yard as high winds lifted the roof from the building and threw it into a house across the street. The lumber yard building was virtually destroyed it. The longest tornado track cut across three counties. The tornado touched down in Boone County and cut a path across southern Story County into northeast Polk County. This tornado had a very intermittent track and lifted several times or remained just above ground. As it moved across northeast Polk County, the storm weakened. Damage was limited due to its intermittent track and the fact that that part of the state is not heavily populated. The storm moved into Jasper County, but by then was below severe levels and just produced heavy rainfall and some small hail. During the late night hours, two tornadoes touched down in Scott County. One north of New Liberty was only a brief touch down and caused no significant damage. The second was north of the Stockton area. A couple was camping in Scott County north of Stockton. The tornado rolled their mobile home. The husband received several cuts and bruises. His wife sustained a broken arm and cuts that required 24 stitches.

A touchdown then occurred 2 miles southwest of Laura on State Route 721 and again 1 mile southeast of Ditmer Road and again 2 miles southeast of Shiloh Road. overview: A warm frontal boundary was to the south of Iowa during the afternoon. Funnel clouds were reported in the central and east central counties. Intense thunderstorms erupted over the east central counties, however only one produced severe weather in central Iowa, and a second in the east central counties. Severe thunderstorms hit southern Wisconsin with a variety of weather including one tornado, violent Thunderstorm wind to 66 mph and heavy rain which caused extensive flash flooding in many counties. The tornado set down on a farm one mile west of Genoa City in Walworth County moving a silo off its foundation and damaging a horse barn and 25 trees. Violent thunderstorms winds knocked down numerous trees and power lines as well as blowing down grain bins in Campbellsport (Fond du Lac County), a barn in Whitelaw (Manitowoc County) and causing roof damage in Two Rivers (Manitowoc County). Rainfall amounts of three to seven inches allowed the Black Earth Creek to overflow its banks, flooding the towns of Mazomanie (Dane County) and Black Earth (Dane County). The Little Platte river flooded parts of Platteville (Grant County). Bonner Creek overflowed flooding part of the town of Belmont (Lafayette yette County) including a lumberyard. Water poured out of Tarrant Lake and rushed into Cambria (Columbia County) flooding a factory, several businesses, roads and homes. Apple Creek near DePere (Brown County) spilled over its banks flooding a campground. In Fond du Lac (Fond du Lac County) the Fond du Lac River flooded nine homes after leaving its banks. Numerous highways and secondary roads were washed out or flooded for extended periods of time in other counties.

A tornado touched down on the north side of Mackinac Island. The tornado path was from British Landing on the northwest side of the island northeast to the other side of the island near Scotts Shore road. Aerial survey indicated total destruction of trees in some areas and other areas where the tops of the trees were destroyed. Less than 50 percent of the path had destruction. Ground survey indicated trees in some areas had fallen down in different directions. Some trees were also uprooted.

A tornado touched down on the west side of Mackinaw Island. The tornado path was in a north to south line mostly near the dirt road called Forest Way. The path extended from 3/4 mile south of British Landing to 1/4 mile south of British Landing. Some trees were uprooted and some were broken and twisted along the path. Buildings in this area has some damage to roofs due to fallen trees. Trees up to 25 inches in diameter were destroyed. Only about 10 percent of the path had destruction. One minor injury was reported from flying glass due to the wind. Power was out in the affected areas for 14 to 16 hours.

A cold air funnel touched down and destroyed a shed on the airport.
A tornado skipped along a path from the northwest shore of Lake Owasso to just north of Interstate 694. Several homes and garages sustained damage and many large trees were uprooted.

overview: Thunderstorms erupted ahead of a warm front as it moved north into Iowa. The storms moved into west central and central Iowa, Hail in excess of two inches in diameter caused damage in Little Sioux in Harrison County. A small tornado touched down in Audubon County west of Audubon. It struck one farm, taking down several trees and destroying the barn. A funnel cloud was also sighted in Mills County, west of Glenwood. There were scattered reports of high winds with some of the storms. In Shelby County, a farm was damaged by high winds in the Portsmouth area. In the later stages of the event, heavy rainfall occurred in Dallas County. Two to three inches of rain fell in under two hours on already saturated ground. Water quickly filled ditches and overtopped roads around the county. Thunderstorms that preceded the main area of activity moved across the Ames area in Story County. Lightning struck a workshop two miles south of Ames setting it ablaze. The shop was destroyed. Later in the morning, the area of thunderstorms moved into east central Iowa. Only one report of severe weather was received as three-quarter inch diameter hail fell southwest of Muscatine.

details: A small tornado touched down in the Washington County Town of Granville where several trees were uprooted. One of the trees fell on a house causing damage to the roof. A hay barn was pushed off its foundation while another barn had its tin roof pulled off and two one-ton wagons were overturned.

Numerous buildings and homes sustained roof damage. Trees and signs were blown down. A grain elevator was blown over. At least 12 utility poles were knocked down. The most severe damage was to a three story apartment building. The wall of the top floor was blown in and the roof collapsed.

The back of a salt storage silo was blown off by small tornado. State police reported that the tornado touched down at mile marker 91 on Interstate 39 near Interstate 88. Two cars were damaged by flying debris.

overview: A cold front began moving into Iowa from the northwest. Copious amounts of moisture was available for this event with precipitable water values around two inches. Thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon hours. By the early evening the storms had formed into a well developed mesoscale convective system. The main feature with the storms was the heavy rainfall, however there was some severe weather associated with the storms during the event. Golf ball-size hail pelted the area around Schleswig in Crawford County. In fact, baseball-size hail to the south of Schleswig caused total crop destruction in the area. The largest hail reported was in Harrison County at Little Sioux. Hail reached three inches in diameter causing considerable crop damage. In Dow City, also in Crawford County, high winds in what appeared to be a microburst struck. A farm was leveled by winds around 85 MPH. High winds were also reported in Carroll County in the city of Carroll. Minor damage occurred in Decatur City in Decatur County during the decaying stages of the system. There were a few tornadoes spawned by the system. They were each quite small and were only on the ground for a short period of time. One tornado touched down in Crawford County south of Vail. The tornado downed several trees and destroyed a few out buildings. Another tornado touched down near Boone in an open field, causing little damage. A similar situation occurred in Greene County west of Jefferson as well as in Chickasaw County north of New Hampton. One of the storms became rather intense and produced a tornado that was on the ground in Dallas County for several miles. Little damage was reported as the tornado passed between several farmsteads. The same storm cluster later produced a funnel cloud over the northeast part of Des Moines. Reports indicated the funnel was very near touching the ground. Other reports of funnel clouds were received from Cherokee County, where four of them were observed west of Cherokee. A few funnel cloud reports were also received from the surrounding counties, but there were no touch downs. Extremely heavy rainfall was reported in Audubon, Crawford, Carroll, and Greene Counties. Damage was very heavy in Crawford County. Initial reports showed that damage in the county was in the $3-4 million range. Story County was also hard hit as 2 1/2 to 5 inches of rain fell across the Squaw Creek basin. Flooding was severe in Ames, with the creek reaching an all time high. Damage to Iowa State University was in the millions of dollars. The Skunk River also rose markedly, causing additional problems, and eventually closing Interstate 35 fora while. The heaviest rainfall was reported around Coon Rapids with 7.83 inches falling in a few hours time. There were numerous reports of three to seven inch rainfall amounts. Manilla reported 7.50 inches of rainfall, with nearly that amount in Denison. Unofficial amounts were higher. In Greene County, the city of Scranton reported 11 inches of rainfall, while ten inches was reported in Carroll County at Willey. In Crawford County, damage from flash flooding was estimated at $15 million. Severe flood damage occurred in 50 homes in Denison and 36 in Dow City. The water rose so quickly that reports indicated that some homes flooded in as little at 11 minutes. Monona County was also hard hit, with rainfall in the four to nine inch range from Onawa east into Harrison County. Damage was extensive in Shelby County where the flood waters washed out several bridges. Highway 59 was under water two miles south of Defiance. Highway 191 was closed between Earling and Panama by flooding from Mosquito Creek. Two hundred and fifty people were forced out of a mobile home park in Harlan, where the water and sewage plant was flooded. Water ran three feet deep in Irwin. Heavy rainfall in excess of three inches fell across much of the north half of the Raccoon River Basin, and extended into the middle Des Moines River Basin. These rains closed numerous roads and washed out bridges in several counties. At one time the Crawford County sheriff reported that nearly all roads in the county were closed by high water. The heavy rainfall set the stage for what was to become the flood of record along the Raccoon and Des Moines River. Flash flooding also occurred east of this area along much of the line of thunderstorms. The flooding extended on a scattered basis all the way to the northeast part of the state. Some of the heavier rains fell in Tama County. Four inches of rain fell resulting in water in the streets of Tama and Chelsea of seven feet in depth.

overview: Southern Iowa was ahead of the cold front in the warm sector. During the evening hours a Derecho formed over southern Nebraska. The Derecho races across southern Nebraska and southern Iowa at 50 to 60 knots. High winds in the 70 to 100 MPH range were reported with the system. As the storms moved into Iowa, a Bow Echo formed on the lead edge. High winds of 90 to 100 MPH downed 13 high tension power line poles in the eastern part of Council Bluffs. Winds of at least 85 MPH ripped into Fremont County, blowing a church off of its foundation in Bartlett. Considerable tree and building structural damage was reported across the southwest quarter of the state. As an example, roof damage was reported to one house and garage with windows blown in at Pilot Grove Park in Montgomery County, with a shed and barn leveled in Page County near Bethesda. There were two injuries as the storms rolled through. One was south of Glenwood in Mills County as a woman sustained minor injuries from flying debris. Another woman was cut by flying glass near Portsmouth as high winds ripped through the area. Other damage in southwest Iowa included the roof being blown off of a house south of Glenwood and another roof taken off of a mobile home hear Hastings. High winds uprooted trees in Red Oak in Montgomery County. Five miles east of Elliot, a house had windows blown out and damage was done to the roof. As the storms moved into Des Moines, high winds blew car windows out on the south side of the city. High winds in Warren county picked up a gravity bin wagon north of Lacona and threw it 50 feet. A pontoon boat was tossed 100 feet by high winds near Seymour. A few tornadoes were reported. One was actually a gustnado in Monroe County. Several roofs were damaged and tree tops were taken off in the town of Albia. Another tornado touched down briefly north of Agency in Wapello County. A metal building was completely flattened. In what turned out to be one of the stronger tornadoes, a touchdown was reported in the Portsmouth area. Two houses were damaged extensively. In addition, a mobile home was overturned with the roof taken off of another building. A horse trailer was picked up and carried for 250 feet. Rainfall was heavy with the Derecho, but with the speed of movement the amounts were generally less than an inch. Late in the severe weather episode, general river flooding began. The Boyer River flooded through Harrison County from heavy upstream rains. Homes, businesses, and croplands were flooded including areas around Woodbine and Missouri Valley. Seventy five to 80 homes were flooded in Missouri Valley where water was 3 to 4 feet deep in places. The Missouri River also flooded the Willow Creek Area. The West Nishnabotna River flooded through Pottawattamie County. About 50 people were evacuated in Avoca where water flooded the town to the highest levels since 1947. Interstate 80 was closed in the area for a time on the 9th after water swept a number of cars off the roadway. Downstream, record flooding occurred around the Hancock area where the park was heavily damaged. The crest rolled into the Oakland area early on the 10th, overflowing sand bags and flooding widespread areas of the town. Numerous roads were flooded and bridges damaged. Crop damage was heavy. The Missouri River also overflowed, forcing evacuations at Goose Haven and Honey Creek. In Mills and Fremont Counties, the West Nishnabotna River flooded croplands and roads throughout the area, damaging some bridges. Some overflows affected the area around Hastings.

overview: Thunderstorms fired up across northern Iowa in a very moist and unstable atmosphere. They were ahead of an approaching cold front. The storms fired during the early afternoon hours. They tracked across northern Iowa into the east-central counties. A few tornadoes were spawned by the stronger storms. One touched down briefly in Cerro Gordo County. The second touched down in Floyd County. This tornado was on the ground for about 12 mifes and caused damage to a few farmsteads. For the most part the storms caused high winds, at times gusting to around 80 MPH. Winds gusted to 80 MPH in Ogden, in Boone County. Numerous reports of trees and power lines being downed by the high winds were received. Early in the storms development, large hail was reported in northwest Iowa. Baseball and larger size hail fell in Lyon and Sioux Counties with a swath of 90% crop damage from northwest to southeast of Boydon. All of the windows on the north side of the houses in Boydon were broken by the hail. Other reports of hail were received after these initial reports. Most of the hail was pea to marble-size. Three-quarter inch diameter hail fell in Winneshiek County at Decorah, while the largest hail report was in Webster County. Callender reported golf ball to softball-size hail briefly. Crops were destroyed and leaves stripped off of trees in the area. The combination of the hail and three inches of rainfall caused large drifts of hail. High winds resulted in an injury in Floyd County. An 11 year old was injured at a campground as a tree branch fell on his leg. In Palo Alto County, lightning struck a golf cart shed at a local golf course. It started a fire that destroyed the shed and several carts.

overview: The synoptic situation was set up a little differently than that of the past several days. The warm front had moved north into Iowa, however several old outflow boundaries remained from the past days convection. There were three main differences in the pattern on this day as compared with the previous several. The first was that a strong low level jet became established during the evening. What was on the order of 30 kts by late afternoon increased to 50 to 60 kts during the evening. This was stronger than the low level jet of the past several days. A cold front was approaching, which also aided in the formation of convection. The third factor was a strong short wave, or upper air disturbance, approaching the area. These factors combined to set of explosive thunderstorm development during the late afternoon hours into the evening. The storms first fired up over southeast Nebraska. The storm cluster expanded into a mesoscale convective complex in just three hours time as the low level jet pushed a pool of 75 to 80 degree dew point temperatures into the region. The storms produced copious rainfall over parts of Nebraska. During the early evening a strong line developed on the lead edge of the complex. This line advanced into lowa at nearly 50 kts. This spared lowa of what could have been a flooding/flash flooding event of historical proportions. The speed of movement kept precipitation amounts under two inches in most areas. Heavy rainfall of two inches in a 30 minute time me period was reported in Council Bluffs area. Streets were flooded with numerous intersections under water. A theater was damaged when flood waters crept in. About two feet of water covered the theater's parking lot. The storm complex was tornadic as it moved across southeast Nebraska. Two tornadoes were spawned in southwest Iowa. The first straddled the Mills and Fremont County line south of Glenwood. It was preceded by two funnel cloud reports in Fremont County about 20 minutes prior to touchdown. The tornado damaged trees and caused considerable damage to a mobile home east of Bartlett. The main feature with the storms was high winds. A few funnel clouds were reported over southwest Iowa during the early stages of the event. They were reported in both Page and Adams Counties. A small tornado touched down briefly in the town of Corning about an hour before. The funnel cloud came from a secondary storm that developed. The storms did produce some small hail in the Moville area of Woodbury County. Reports of winds of 70 MPH or more were numerous. Tree and power line damage was quite widespread. In Woodbury County northwest of Climbing Hill, high winds downed power lines and damaged a hog shed on one farm. Sheet metal was strewn across the road there. High winds struck southeast of the town of Treynor in Pottawattamie County. The 75 MPH winds downed several barns and damaged outbuildings in the area. Two farms south of Walnut sustained heavy damage from the thunderstorm winds. A roof was lifted off one farmhouse. A large metal storage shed was twisted and smashed. A barn was destroyed and several grain bins were lifted. The storms high winds downed a barn south of Creston, in Union County. Considerable damage was reported in Guthrie County. A lot of trees were downed, the roof was taken off of one house, part of the roof on the 4H building, and the roof of the ready mix plant were all taken off in Guthrie Center. A small camper was moved across a parking lot there as well. Needless to say, considerable damage was also done to power lines in the area. As one of the stronger storms moved across the Des Moines Airport, very high winds were recorded. An apparent microburst occurred along with the passage of the gust front. In actuality, the highest winds occurred after the first thunderstorms moved over the airport. An intense storm just to the south of the airport resulted in wind gusts of 83 MPH at the airport. The Air Traffic Control Tower recorded a sustained 89 MPH wind for a period of several minutes. The storms moved east and produced 70 MPH winds in northern Warren County at Carlisle. Significant tree and power line damage was reported in the area. Another isolated wind event occurred in Franklin County at Hampton. Roof damage was reported from several buildings at the Franklin County Fairgrounds, caused by high winds. After midnight, a small cluster of storms formed in southwest Iowa. They became severe and produced high winds in Union County in the Creston area. The area southwest of Creston was hardest hit when high winds leveled a block wide area. Once again, this appeared to be a microburst and not a tornado in spite of the fact that the radar echo tops were in excess of 70,000 feet. The storm continued to move east and produced high winds in Clarke County. Winds downed several trees and some power lines in Osceola. All of the storms produced torrential rains. Flash flooding was minimal due to the speed of movement, however there were some local problems mainly in urban areas. The storms moved east during the night and resulted in damage as they moved through Cedar County. An outbuilding was moved off of its foundation west of Lowden. North of Lowden, shingles were blown off of a house and stuck into the screen in front of a picture window. Several trees were downed in the area as well.

Damage was estimated near 1.5 million dollars.

The tornado first touched down 1 mile northeast of Kenbridge in Lunenburg County at 1243 EDT, where roofs were blown off of a briquet plant and a furniture company building. Damage estimates in Lunenburg County were $300,000.  The tornado moved northeast into southeast Nottoway County and strengthened.  It leveled a barn, some outbuildings and trees on Route 46 near the west edge of Fort Pickett Military Reservation. Damages in Nottoway County were estimated at $100,000.   It continued northeast into Dinwiddie County and the Fort Pickett Military Reservation where it did minimal damage.  It moved northeast to the town of Ford where the most significant damage in the county occurred.  It destroyed a house and a shed and knocked down numerous telephone poles, and large trees.  The tornado tracked northeast into the southeast part of Chesterfield County and lifted about 5 miles west of Colonial Heights.

The most devastating tornado of the day touched down one mile southwest of Petersburg at approximately 1330 EDT.  This tornado rapidly grew in size and strength as it moved northeast into the commercial historic district of Petersburg.  Numerous homes and businesses sustained major damage.  Damage estimates for the area were $15 million.  Forty people were injured. The tornado crossed the river into Colonial Heights and struck one of the area's shopping districts.  It destroyed some buildings and did major damage to numerous other buildings including the the Wal-Mart, where three people were killed and nearly 200 were injured.  Total damage estimates in Colonial Heights were $29.5 million. The tornado crossed the Appomattox River again into Prince George County where it struck a sand and gravel pit company.  A block building collapsed and numerous vehicles and other equipment were destroyed.  One person was killed.  Damage estimates were $750,000.  It then moved into the northern section of Hopewell,  where it ripped into the Riverside Park Apartment Complex, tearing the roofs off of several buildings. Minor damage was done to another 49 homes, major damage to 13 homes and 2 were destroyed.  The tornado weakened then dissipated near the confluence of the Appomattox and James Rivers.  Eight people were reported injured and damage estimates were $2.2 million.  (F48O) (F40O) (F56O) (M28O)

The storm uprooted and twisted off several trees before tearing off part of the roof of the Marple Place apartments.  The Springfield Republican Leader's home was hit hard by the tornado.  More than 20 large trees (some of them were over 200 years old and more than 150 feet tall) came down in his yard, two of which crashed onto the roof of his home on Township Line road.  A large tree also fell through the roof of a two story home on Spring Alley Road in Springfield causing extensive damage to the second floor.  An entire row of large trees were uprooted in front of the Springfield police chief's home on Kerr Lane.  Several other homes and vehicles were damaged by falling trees and blowing debris and cars were moved in the twisters path.  No deaths or injuries were reported.  Additionally, 40,00 customers lost power countywide.

The tornado touched down near Neshaminy High School and moved NE through Langhorne to near Country Club in Yardley.  In addition to numerous trees downed, extensive structural damage occurred as the twisted swept through the county. In one instance, the tornado ripped the roof off of an orchard warehouse on Woodbourne Road in Middletown township.  The roof landed in the road over 100 feet away.  One car in the parking lot was damaged.  As a result of the downed utility poles and trees, 20,000 customers lost power countywide and three schools cancelled classes because of power outages.  Although no injuries resulted from the tornado and associated thunderstorm, in a related incidence, a Bell of PA technician on a repair call in Eastown Township, Chester County, was killed when he came in contact with a downed power line.

Four businesses in West Ridge Shopping Center and two mobile homes in the Wildwood subdivision were destroyed and two outbuildings at a high school damaged.  Total damages were estimated at more than $500,000.

Most of the damaged or destroyed homes were two story with brick or stucco exterior. Several residents noted that the tornado sounded like a freight train as it passed overhead.  One elderly lady stated that her dog became restless and started barking 20 minutes before the tornado struck her home.  Continuous lightning was observed by several residents prior to and after the tornado touchdown.   Several cars were destroyed by fallen trees or wind blown debris. The powerful storm that caused high winds across Oregon also spawned the most powerful tornado in the state in many years.  The tornado occurred as the coldfront associated with a deep surface low along the coast moved across the Willamette Valley in mid-afternoon.  The tornado touched down southeast of Newburg and heavily damaged a dairy farm, toppling large trees, killing six veal calves, and destroying calf shelters.  The tornado then proceeded northeasterly to a horseranch, where roofs were blown off some small buildings and extensive damage was done by flying debris, including some very large trees that were snapped off and uprooted.  The tornado next damaged the roof of a house and some nearby structures and then crossed the Willamette River. Passing motorists reported seeing the funnel sucking water up from the river.  After uprooting more trees and damaging a mobile home, the tornado apparently skipped a few miles northeast where it touched down near a mobile home park and caused extensive damage to mobile homes there. Near the northern end of the twisters path a tree at least 24 inches in diameter was snapped off six feet above ground and, along with other debris, hit a two story home and moved it off its foundation.  Incredibly, no one was injured.

details: A tornado began about one mile south-southwest of Ragland in St. Clair County at 1055 CST and traveled northeast at between 45 and 55 miles an hour crossing the Alabama/Georgia border about five miles northeast of Rock Run in Cherokee County.  The tornado moved across County Highway 144 just south-southwest of Ragland where it first began then destroyed a number of structures along 144 to the east of Ragland.  The tornado crossed primarily wooded land before moving through a camping area on the west side of Neely Henry Lake.  A woman was killed outside on the west side of the lake as she tried to secure a boat.  The tornado crossed Neely Henry Lake just north of the dam as it moved into Calhoun County.  Twenty-six homes were damaged, 18 homes were destroyed, and 20 mobile homes were destroyed in St. Clair County.   Moving into Calhoun County at 1104 CST, the storm continued on a steady northeast track (60 degree heading) crossing the north side of Ohatchee.  The storm crossed U.S. Highway 431 at 1120 CST where one man was killed when the van he was in was thrown into a ditch.  Three other people in the van were injured.  The storm continued northeast across mostly woodlands with only scattered structures, mostly homes, in its path.  It crossed U.S. Highway 278 between four and five miles west-northwest of Piedmont. The storm entered Cherokee County at 1135 CST.  At 1139 CST the tornado destroyed the Goshen United Methodist Church located one mile north of the Cherokee/Calhoun County line on County Highway 9 killing 20 people and injuring 92.  The tornado continued northeast across Cherokee County reaching the Alabama/Georgia state line at approximately 1152 CST. details: A classic spring synoptic situation was taking shape over Iowa.  Intense low pressure moved across western Kansas into southern Nebraska.  A warm front extended east from the low into Iowa.  Warm and moist air was in place over the state.  Surface dew point temperatures were in the lower to middle 60s with significant moisture extending above the 850 mb level.  Meanwhile, drier air was working its way northeast aloft.  Violent thunderstorms erupted during the late afternoon hours over northwest Iowa.  There were several reports of tornadoes just to the north of the Iowa/Minnesota border.  The storms moved into the northwest part of the state and produced hail, high winds, and funnel clouds.  Winds gusted to 63 mph at the Sioux City Gateway Airport.  A short time later three-quarter inch diameter hail pelted the area.  High winds caused damage in Plymouth County around LeMars.  Numerous trees and power lines were downed.  Part of a building was destroyed south of LeMars.  The local utility company recorded a wind gust of 75 mph.  A funnel cloud was sighted a short time earlier west of town.  The storms clipped the far northwest corner of the state as well.  Winds gusted to 78 mph at Sioux Center, causing damage around town.  A funnel cloud was sighted in Lyon County at Alvord.  A tornado also touched down in the area, a short distance east of Alvord.  It struck two farms, causing extensive damage to each.  Several buildings were downed on a farm near Hull, a machine shed, garage, and brooder coop were downed north of Hull.  The storms worked their way northeast.  Hail the size of quarters was reported later in the evening in Kossuth County, southwest of Algona.  During this time, an area of thunderstorms developed over east-central Iowa.  One of them dropped hail the size of quarters at Clarence in Cedar County.  In Henry County, one-inch diameter was recorded at Mt. Pleasant.

details: Thunderstorms had moved out of Iowa for the most part during the late evening hours as the dry slot advanced over the state.  During the early morning hours, three other features combined to once again produce severe weather in the state.  The surface dry line was advancing east across Kansas and southeast Nebraska.  At the same time a strong low level jet had become established with speeds in excess of 55 kts.  Above this a strong jet stream was in place in the upper levels.  What is known as a speed maximum (a jet streak) rotated around the upper trough and ejected toward Iowa.  This set the stage for rekindling of strong thunderstorms.  At this time, moisture was much more limited so thunderstorms were more of the pulse variety and were not able to maintain their strength as in a supercell storm.  Hail and winds were the trademarks of these storms.  Hail of three-quarters of an inch to one inch in diameter pelted Adams and Adair Counties.  Many of the other storms only produced pea- to occasional marble-size hail.  One storm became quiet strong for a while.  It was the southern most storm in the line.  It produced 60 mph winds as it passed through both Greenfield and Corning.  Another storm developed a couple hours later and moved into central Iowa.  High winds blew into the west part of Ames causing damage to trees and buildings.  A tornado developed on the southwest part of the storm a short time later.  It tracked through the western parts of the city.  It touched down near new United States Highway 30 and lifted as it crossed old Highway 30.  Several buildings were damaged or destroyed.  Windows were broken out on several houses and cars in the area.  Power was knocked out in the area as well.

The storm approached the city from the west-southwest.  There were unconfirmed reports of funnels in the Horseshoe Bay area, four miles southwest of Marble Falls, before the storm arrived.  Spotty damage was reported to roofs in the Horseshoe Bay area.  The tornado first struck the west side of the city, crossing a heavy commercialized and residential area.  Roofs were severely damaged at this time with several structures sustaining F1 and F2 damage.  Several boats at a dealership were tossed on top of each other.  Two-by-four's were embedded into the side of a church preschool care center, penetrating an inside classroom wall by four to five feet.  Fortunately, all children had been moved into hallways just before the tornado arrived.  Numerous commerical signs were down with widespread roof damage.  This damage became even more extensive as the tornado moved across the northern part of the city.  Marble Falls primary school also sustained damage, but students had been evacuated to the main school.  Trees were uprooted on the school grounds and damage was reported to outbuildings.  Metal I-beams were bent at a nearby metal building, indicating F2 to F3 damage.  Three nearby semi-tractor trailer delivery trucks and a bread delivery truck were overturned.  Two of these trucks were reported to have been lifted "two to three feet off of the ground" as they were overturned.  At a nearby Wal-Mart department store 100 to 200 employees had taken shelter, having practiced their severe weather drill the day before.  The store was hit and severely damaged, with the employees sustaining only a few minor injuries.  Additional roof damage was reported at Marble Falls High School.  Students had just executed a tornado drill as the storm struck.  There was extensive peeling of metal from the auditorium and gymnasium roofs. In summary, over 440 homes sustained damage, with one house and 17 mobile homes destroyed and major damage to 36 homes.  Eighteen businesses reported major damage with 47 others reporting minor damage.  In addition, two bridges were damaged, along with severe damage to schools.  In all, 512 structures sustained damage.

details: An F2 tornado touched down one mile south of Pocahontas and traveled south-southeastward for approximately two miles before lifting. An F1 tornado touched down about 2.5 miles south-southeast of Brinkley and traveled approximately 5 miles before lifting.  Thirteen large electrical transmission towers were damaged or destroyed.  Large power lines fell onto U.S. Highway 49.  Smaller power lines were also blown down along the tornado's path, as were a few trees.  Several grain storage bins were destroyed.  No injuries were reported.

A F1 (Fujita Scale) tornado touched down in the Blackwood area of Gloucester Township in Camden County.  The tornado touched down along Davistown Road where a large tree was uprooted and a five foot diameter maple tree was snapped.  Damage continued northeast across Brooklyn Road to the Heinz Bakery Plant on Little Gloucester Road.  Silo caps, roof vents and roof tar paper were either blown or peeled off.  The greatest damage and area of maximum tornadic strength was inflicted upon the Kindercare Learning Center on Broadacres Drive.  Fortunately this occurred on a Sunday and none of the usual 100 children were inside.  Pine trees near the center were uprooted.  Most of the roof of the center was lifted off.  Aluminum siding was peeled off.  Insulation and siding were found in trees 200 yards from the center.  Its central air conditioning unit was blown 20 yards.  Several chain link fences near the center were turned down and a dumpster was flipped over.  Two trailers sitting on a loading dock of a supermarket near the Kindercare Center were blown over.  The supermarket's roof ventilation system also sustained damage. The last tornado related damaged occurred about one quarter of a mile northeast of the Kindercare where large limbs were snapped off.  No injuries were reported.

details: A tornado downed large trees from Jeannette to Greensburg, closing State Route 30.  An apartment roof was blown off at Greensburg, leaving eight families homeless.  Other buildings sustained minor damage.  Structural damage was estimated at $428,000.

A tornado touched down in Beaver Creek Township just north of Seven-Mile Road, about 1.5 miles west of Military Road.  It moved generally eastward, along the north side of Seven-Mile Road, doing widespread tree damage.  At about the time the tornado crossed Military Road, it appears to have dissipated as another vortex from the same parent cloud formed just south of Seven-Mile Road.  The newly strengthened tornado then continued its movement east, crossing the U.S. 27 expressway, damaging the roofs of three houses and blowing over numerous large trees before it lifted, just after crossing Interstate 75.  In all, more than 1,000 trees were destroyed, and at least five residences suffered some degree of damage.  The worst damage was done to a residence along South Grayling Road, where virtually all of the large oaks around the house were torn down, doing extensive roof damage estimated at around $8,000.  The tornado stripped bare the roof of an old motel just west of Old U.S. 27 Highway.

details: Strong upper air dynamics combined with a cold front moved into Iowa.  The airmass remained very unstable with surface dew point temperatures in the lower to middle 70s.  The moisture layer was deep with 850 mb dew point temperatures around 15�� C.  Thunderstorms occurred during the early morning hours over western Iowa.  The outflow boundary from that complex advanced into the central part of the state by sunrise.  Thunderstorms developed throughout the day along this outflow boundary.  During the afternoon hours they became severe.  Several tornadoes were spawned.  Two weak tornadoes touched down briefly in north central Iowa.  One was in Winnebago County, the other in Worth County.  Neither of them caused any significant damage as they occurred in open country.  A fairly strong tornado touched down in Chickasaw County.  The tornado touched down southwest of New Hampton and tracked northeast.  It his a truck repair shop at the intersection of U.S. Highway 63 and County Highway B54.  The roof was removed from the repair facility.  Most of the tornado track was through open country, which kept damage to a minimum.  The same parent storm caused high winds at the intersection of U.S. Highway 63 and Iowa Highway 18.  The winds removed the roof from a car wash there and also damaged several cars in the parking lot there.  Debris from the tornado broke windows and punctured the tires on two trucks in the lot.  Another tornado made a cameo touchdown in a field north of Clermont in Fayette County.  In addition to the tornadoes, there were a few other funnel cloud reports.  None of these touched down to become tornadoes.  Many of the storms over the east half of the state produced gusty winds and small hail.  Only a few were strong enough to become severe.  One storm caused wind damage in Bremer County.  High winds blew the roof off of a barn and downed trees and power lines south of Plainfield.  Another storm uprooted several trees in Waverly.  Damage of $10,000-$15,000 was reported in Fredericksburg as high winds damaged the roof of a service station.

details: A rare (with respect to both time of day and intensity) tornado  outbreak affected eastern Chester County the evening of the 27th. Tornadic thunderstorms affected portions of the Middle Atlantic States south of Pennsylvania earlier that evening.  As the first thunderstorm moved into southeast Chester County, it dropped its first tornado in London Britain Township near New London Road about 9:55 pm EST.  The    tornado reached its maximum intensity (F3 on the Fujita Scale) and destruction in the Hunter's Run Development on Crestwood Road.  Six homes were destroyed and twenty-three were damaged.  Eleven persons were injured.  A 40-year-old man was critically injured when he was blown through his 2nd story window.  Two teenagers were injured when a tree landed on their Ford Ranger Pickup.  The rest of the injuries were mainly from flying glass.  A gentleman's credit cards from London Britain were found 30 miles away.  Heavy damage was reported along Chesterville Road as the tornado passed into New Garden Township.  The worst damage in New Garden Township occurred to mushroom houses on Penn Green and Starr Roads.  Eleven mushroom houses were damaged, three had their roofs torn off, eight had collapsed walls. Although the tornado lifted close to Starr Road in New Garden Township, downburst wind damage continued father north into neighboring townships.  Even to the east of the tornado in London Britain Township, damaging wind gusts did massive damage in the White Clay Preserve and trees and wires were down on half the roads within the township.  Farther north thunderstorm downburst winds ripped the roof off a hanger in the New Garden Airport and damaged the roof of the Unionville Elementary School in East Marlborough Township.  Downed trees forced the closures of U.S. Routes 1 and 322 and Pennsylvania State Routes 41 and 162. Thunderstorm wind related damage continued north into Newlin Township and as the thunderstorm moved north into West Bradford, it dropped its second Chester County tornado of the evening.  The weaker (F1 on the Fujita Scale) tornado touched down about 10:20 pm EST near the intersection of Telegraph and Sugarbridge Roads and uprooted trees.  A mobile home on Sugar Bridge Road suffered severe damage to its porch and roof as a tree fell on it.  The tornado followed a discontinuous path through West Bradford and northern East Bradford Township before lifting near the intersection of Boot and Valley Creek Roads.  Most of the damage was uprooted trees and downed chimneys. Thunderstorm related wind damage was then reported in Downingtown with two foot diameter trees uprooted.  As the thunderstorm headed north, wind related damage diminished.  Just before it left Chester County, the thunderstorm split in two and the westward one entered Montgomery County near Limerick. The Chester County Office of Emergency Management estimated total damage in the county at $3.5 million with 9 houses or buildings totally destroyed and 49 other sustaining slight or moderate damage.

details: The parent thunderstorm that produced two tornadoes and downburst wind damage in eastern Chester County split in two near Spring City in Chester County.  The left or western thunderstorm entered Montgomery County in Royersford and wind related damage intensified as the thunderstorm moved northeast through Royersford.  Most of the damage  (collapsed porches and downed trees) in Royerstown occurred from Fifth Avenue to Lewis Road and from Main to Chestnut Streets  Several homes were damaged by falling trees.  Lewis Road was closed for two days because of tree removal. From police and eyewitness reports apparently a funnel cloud was working its way toward the ground over Royersford and became a tornado in Limerick just to the northeast of Linfield Road at 10:45 pm EST.  The tornado intensified into a strong (F3 on the Fujita Scale) one as it paralleled Limerick Road on its western side.  A development called "The Hamlet" was in the direct path of this tornado.  The Hamlet was a new development started within the past 2 years and about 30 of the planned 430 units were occupied or under construction.  The  development took a direct hit from the tornado.  This resulted in 3 deaths (the same family) and 25 injuries.  Of the 27 inhabited houses, 4 were leveled, 16 were damaged beyond repair, 1 under construction was destroyed and only 7 remained liveable.  Damage in this development alone was $2 million.  The family of three which lost their lives lived on Victory Way.  They were asleep and blown out of their house.  The father was found on the front lawn.  The mother and her 10-month-old daughter were found over a sewer grate.  A United States Savings Bond in the child's name was found the next day in Bath, Pennsylvania.  Bath is located about 50 miles northeast in Northampton County.  Another man was blown through the second story window of his house about 50 feet into the family room of his neighbor's house and survived.  Equally miraculous a 5-month-old infant sailed out of his crib onto the front lawn of his home and survived. As tragic as the devastation was at "The Hamlet", it was not the only place in Limerick to sustain damage.  As the tornado traveled through the business area of the town,  it leveled most of the Hide and Seek Storage Sheds (damage estimated at $1 million). It peeled part of the roof off the Limerick Diner.  None of the 30 patrons inside  were injured.  The Atlantic and Sunoco Gas Stations sustained major damage.  Gasoline pumps at the Sunoco Station were wrenched from their cement foundation.  An overturned beige truck lay about 200 yards from where it was parked.  Even the Limerick Fire House sustained about $25,000 in wind damage.  In addition to "The Hamlet", 14 other homes in Limerick sustained major damage.  About 90 persons in Limerick had to find temporary shelter.  Total damage in Limerick alone was estimated between $5 and $5.5 million. The tornado lifted in the Limerick Garden of Memories Cemetery, but its parent thunderstorm continued to produce wind related damage in upper (northwestern) Montgomery County.  Downed trees were reported in Zieglersville.  In Marlboro Township about 50 to 60 trees were uprooted on Swamp Creek and Miller Roads.  About 10 properties were damaged by the falling trees, including one house that had six trees on top of it.  A lightning ignited fire extensively damaged a West Marlborough home.  It took six fire companies to get it under control. (M28P), (F28P), (F1P)

Thunderstorms were numerous over Iowa throughout the day.  Several weather features caused the continual development.  There was an upper level disturbance approaching from the west, while a trough of low pressure approached from the northwest.  Farther  northwest was an approaching arctic cold front.  The atmosphere was very moist with deep moisture in place and convective available potential energy between 3000 and 3500 J-Kg-1 over much of the state.  Even so, the situation was not overly conducive to severe weather.  Thunderstorms moved over the west half of the state during the morning hours.  The east half remained under partly sunny skies with thunderstorms erupting during the early afternoon hours, once the weak cap had broken.  The storms produced heavy rainfall and some gusty winds.  Only a few became severe.  A severe thunderstorm moved through Winfield in Henry County, downing several trees.  Another storm produced a brief microburst south of Newton in Jasper County.  Many large tree limbs, up to 20 inches in diameter, were torn off.  Crops were flattened in a narrow strip for about a mile downstream.  Another storm produced a brief spin up tornado in Benton County.  The tornado was observed by a boater as it touched down on Rogers Park Lake.  It sucked up water briefly before breaking apart.  One could call it a waterspout since it did occur over water, however meteorologically it had thunderstorm structure of a land event.  For that reason it was listed as a tornado instead of a waterspout.  During the morning, thunderstorms moved through Clarion.  Lightning struck the chimney of the elementary school.  Several blocks were knocked out of the top of it and the chimney was cracked all the way down to its junction with the main building.
Outbuilding demolished and mobile home damaged.
